opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the hardest questions in research organizations, and I don't think there's a single formula. My view is that it depends a lot on what stage the field is in.

When the direction is still unclear, when nobody really knows which approach will work, bottom-up freedom is extremely valuable. Many of the most important ideas in AI didn't come from a plan written at the top. They came from someone who was curious, tried something a bit weird, and found it worked better than expected. If you over-manage at that stage, you kill exactly the exploration you need. People start optimizing for what their manager wants to see rather than what they actually believe is interesting.

But once a direction is validated, once you see a clear signal that something scales, the game changes. Then it becomes more of an engineering and coordination problem. You need many people working on the same thing, sharing infrastructure, sharing compute, and making trade-offs together. Pure bottom-up freedom at that point can become fragmentation: everyone has their own small project, compute gets spread thin, and nothing gets pushed to the level where it really matters. So you need someone with a strong conviction to say, "This is the bet, let's concentrate resources here."

So the way I think about it is: top-down should mostly decide where to concentrate resources and what the big bets are, while bottom-up should drive how problems get solved and should keep a portion of the organization exploring things that aren't yet in the main bet. A healthy organization keeps some slack, some people and compute that aren't fully allocated, so new signals can emerge.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this balance only works if information flows well. Leadership needs to be close enough to the actual research to recognize when a bottom-up idea is real, and researchers need to understand the reasoning behind top-down decisions rather than just receiving orders. When people understand why the bet is the bet, they often self-align, and you need much less control. In that sense, culture and taste matter more than structure. If the people have good research taste and share a sense of what matters, you can give a lot of freedom and still move in roughly the same direction.

r001.rationale: It says pure bottom-up freedom can cause fragmentation, spread compute thin, and prevent projects from reaching meaningful scale.

r002.rationale: It discusses leadership and research taste, but does not argue that the balance ultimately depends on a technical leader.

r003.rationale: It describes keeping slack for exploration and adapting to the field’s stage, but does not characterize the most innovative organizational state as unstable.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it's less a question of ratio and more a question of what each layer is responsible for. Top-down should set the problem, not the solution. Bottom-up should own the solution, and sometimes get to argue about the problem.

Let me explain what I mean through research, because that's the world I know best. When I was doing my PhD, the most productive moments weren't when my advisor told me exactly what to do, and they weren't when I was completely alone either. They were when there was a very clear, very ambitious north star - say, "we want language models that can actually act in the world, not just talk" - and then almost total freedom in how to get there. ReAct, Tree of Thoughts, those came out of that kind of setup. Nobody assigned them to me. But they also didn't come from nowhere; they came from a shared sense of what mattered.

So the top-down part I'd describe as taste. An organization's leadership has to supply taste: what problems are worth working on, what counts as a real result versus a toy result, what timescale we're playing on. That's genuinely hard, and most organizations under-invest in it. They either give no direction, which produces a lot of locally interesting but globally irrelevant work, or they over-specify, which produces compliance instead of discovery.

The bottom-up part is where the actual information lives. The people closest to the experiments know things leadership can't know yet. In AI especially, the gap between what seems like it should work and what actually works is enormous, and it's only visible from the ground. If you don't give people freedom there, you're throwing away your most valuable signal.

Now, there's a subtlety. Freedom isn't the same as absence of structure. I think the best environments have very strong shared infrastructure, shared evaluation, shared vocabulary, so that bottom-up exploration is legible to everyone else. Otherwise freedom just becomes fragmentation. You end up with twenty people doing twenty things that can't be compared or combined. At OpenAI and at Anthropic, a lot of what makes research move fast is actually quite boring: common codebases, common benchmarks, a culture of writing things down. That's top-down in form but it enables bottom-up in substance.

The other thing I'd say is that the balance should shift over time, and most organizations get the direction of the shift wrong. Early in a research direction, when nobody knows what works, you want to be very bottom-up: lots of small bets, high variance, tolerate a lot of failure. Later, when something has clearly worked and the question becomes scaling it, you need to become much more top-down, because coordination starts to matter more than exploration. Companies often do the reverse. They're rigid when they should be exploring and chaotic when they should be executing.

And finally, I'd push back a little on the framing that the goal is to "stimulate innovation." I don't think innovation is something you stimulate. It's more that you remove the things that suppress it. Fear of being wrong. Having to justify every week. Metrics that reward incremental progress over risky progress. If you take those away and give people a good problem and good colleagues, they'll innovate on their own. The top-down job is mostly to protect that space, not to fill it.

r001.rationale: The response says unrestricted freedom can lead to fragmentation, with people pursuing work that cannot be compared or combined.

r002.rationale: It assigns leadership a role in setting direction and protecting space, but does not argue that the balance ultimately depends on a technical leader.

r003.rationale: It describes early exploration as high-variance and failure-tolerant, but does not characterize the innovation-conducive organizational state as especially unstable.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to be clear about the problem, but leave room for people to discover the solution. Top-down direction is useful for saying, “This matters, and we’re willing to commit resources to it.” It becomes less useful when it also prescribes every step, especially in research, where you don’t yet know which approach will work.

Bottom-up freedom lets people pursue something they’ve noticed before they can fully explain why it matters. But freedom needs support: time, resources, and a way for a small experiment to become a larger effort when the evidence is promising. Otherwise, you have permission to explore, but no practical path to make an impact.

So I’d think of it as a feedback loop. Leadership provides direction; people explore and bring back evidence; that evidence can change the direction. You need enough alignment to work together, and enough openness that someone can discover that the original plan was wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes bottom-up freedom as needing support and a path to scale promising experiments, but does not say that a fully bottom-up approach can cause organizational chaos.

r002.rationale: It discusses leadership providing direction, but does not say the balance ultimately depends on the technical leader.

r003.rationale: The response recommends a feedback loop and openness, but does not characterize the most innovation-conducive organizational state as unstable.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to be clear about what needs alignment and what needs freedom. Leadership should give people a shared sense of which problems matter and why. But if it also prescribes every step toward solving them, there’s very little room left for discovery.

For research, especially, you often don’t know the right approach in advance. So people need space to try something that doesn’t yet fit the roadmap, and to bring back evidence that might change the roadmap itself. That makes the relationship two-way: direction helps people choose useful experiments, and experiments help leadership choose better directions.

You also need some way for a small idea to grow. Giving someone freedom to explore doesn’t mean much if a promising result can never get more resources. I’d start with small, relatively independent experiments, then concentrate support when something starts to work. The balance can change with the stage of the work: more freedom when you’re exploring, more coordination when you’re trying to turn a discovery into something reliable.

r001.rationale: It recommends shared direction alongside freedom, but does not say that fully bottom-up innovation can cause organizational chaos.

r002.rationale: It discusses leadership’s role in setting direction and allocating support, but does not say the balance ultimately depends on the technical leader.

r003.rationale: It says the balance can change by stage of work, but does not characterize an innovation-conducive organizational state as unstable.
